newsitem.title: CANADA: Huge Alberta natgas pool still waiting to be found.
newsitem.headline: Huge Alberta natgas pool still waiting to be found.

text.p: Somewhere in Alberta, where thousands of natural gas wells already dot the landscape, the province's biggest gas pool is still waiting to be discovered, says an independent group of geologists and engineers.

That pool, likely to be found in western Alberta, could hold a prize of four trillion cubic feet of gas, equal to about five percent of all the gas that has been produced to date in western Canada, said Bob Meneley, a member of the Canadian Gas Potential Committee.

Meneley, whose organization on Thursday released a report on Canada's total potential for gas reserves, said several energy companies that reviewed its estimates agreed the elusive monster pool was still out there in the country's most explored region, the Western Canadian Sedimentary Basin.
"They thought that was a reasonable expectation," he said at a media briefing. "Of course, nobody in their right mind is going to tell you where they think it is."

The biggest gas pool found to date in the basin, which includes Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia and the Northwest Territories, was the 3.6 trillion cubic foot Kaybob South pool in northwestern Alberta.
Kaybob South was discovered by Hudson Bay Oil & Gas in 1961.
Committee members said the next big pool was likely in the Leduc geological zone, in Upper Devonian age rock. The medium-to-deep Devonian has long been a mainstay of Alberta gas production.
Throughout Canada, natural gas reserves had the potential to keep supply pumping for at least a century, the Natural Gas Potential in Canada report said.

The committee estimated total reserves in the country at 570 trillion cubic feet, representing 50 years of conventional supply and 50 years of unconventional supply, like colbed methane, using a production rate of 5.5 trillion cubic feet a year.
The study predicted Canada had about 237 trillion cubic feet of discovered gas in place and 207 trillion cubic feet of potential gas in place in the Western Canadian Sedimentary basin.
Of the region's total undiscovered gas potential, 80 percent was estimated to be in Alberta, 15 percent in B.C. and the rest in Saskatchewan, N.W.T. and Yukon.

In Canada's frontier regions, which include the Mackenzie Valley, Beaufort Basin and Sverdrup Basin in the far north and Sable Sub-Basin on the east coast, potential marketable gas reserves were estimated at 107 trillion cubic feet.
The study did not take into account economic cutoffs, or the market prices that would be required to produce gas from the more remote or technically difficult reserves.
The Canadian Gas Potential Committee is made up of senior geoscientists with private and public sector experience and is affiliated with the University of Calgary.
It plans to update its report every three or four years. ((Jeffrey Jones, Reuters Calgary Bureau (403) 531-1624))
